title: Assessment
text:
Grading
Everything is out of 100 marks, with bonus marks on top.

ComponentMarksHow

Project40In groups of four or fewer: proposal report (5), phase I presentation (5), phase II presentation (5), three-minute pitch in the style of 3MT (5), demo and poster (15) and final report (5).
Homework32Eight programming assignments, 4 marks each. Late submissions earn 50% credit: up to one day late for the first assignment and up to two days for the others. A subset has an associated viva.
End semester10Written exam.
Quizzes6Three surprise quizzes worth 3 marks each; the best two count.
Paper presentation4Three students per paper: one summarises it, one argues for it, one acts as devil's advocate. Paper list · slides template.
Kaggle competition4Done individually, due in early April.
ML demo4An interactive demo, in the same team as the project, due 30 March. Examples: k-means, a visual introduction to ML, linear regression, random forests.
Total100Bonus: 10 marks for reaching Master level on Kaggle, or 5 marks for Expert level.

Machine Learning
ES 654 · IIT Gandhinagar · Semester II, 2018–19
ES 654 introduces machine learning from decision trees and ensembles through linear models and optimisation, nearest neighbours, Bayesian estimation and active learning, to support vector machines and neural networks. Students read and argued about research papers, built a demo, entered a Kaggle competition and carried out a group project.

  InstructorProf. Nipun Batra
  Emailnipun.batra@iitgn.ac.in
  ClassesTuesday and Friday, 3:30–5:00 pm, 1/101
  Office hoursMonday, 12:00–1:00 pm
  Teaching assistants4 TAs
  PrerequisitesGood experience in Python programming, probability and linear algebra



Course record
This offering ran from January to April 2019. Its slides, notebooks, homework and exam solutions remain available.

  Lectures26
  Homework8 assignments
  QuizzesSolutions to quizzes 1 and 3
  End semesterExam and answers
  NotebooksOn GitHub

All dates


Lectures

  1–4Foundations and decision trees4 lectures
  5–14Linear models and optimisation10 lectures
  15–19Neighbours, Bayes and active learning5 lectures
  20–26SVMs, logistic regression and neural networks7 lectures


  All 26 lectures




Questions
Is there a project?Yes: a group project in teams of up to four, worth 40%, assessed through a proposal, two presentations, a three-minute pitch, a demo and poster, and a final report. Ideas: from the instructors and from a Stanford ML course.
How do paper presentations work?Three students take each paper: one summarises it, one argues for it, and one acts as devil's advocate, convincing the jury that the paper has flaws. See the paper list and the slides template.
Can I submit homework late?For 50% credit: up to one day late for the first assignment and up to two days for the others. A subset of assignments has a viva.
How do I prepare before the course?Refresh the prerequisites with the first four chapters of the Python Data Science Handbook, some material on linear algebra and Khan Academy's statistics and probability course.

References
Reference textbooks:

  Gareth James, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie and Robert Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R (online)
  Christopher M. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Springer, 2006 (free PDF)
  Jerome Friedman, Trevor Hastie and Robert Tibshirani, The Elements of Statistical Learning, Springer, 2001 (free PDF)
  Richard O. Duda, Peter E. Hart and David G. Stork, Pattern Classification, Wiley, 2012
  Tom M. Mitchell, Machine Learning, McGraw Hill, 1997
  Kevin P. Murphy, Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective, MIT Press
  Ian Goodfellow, Yoshua Bengio and Aaron Courville, Deep Learning, MIT Press, 2016 (online)

Other ML courses:

  NPTEL course by Balaraman Ravindran
  CMU course by Tom Mitchell and Maria-Florina Balcan
  Coursera course by Andrew Ng
  fast.ai course on ML and Practical deep learning for coders
  Course by Alex Ihler, UCI
